questions.q: A shopkeeper pushes a crate of rice 3 m across the floor with a constant force of 40 N in the direction of its motion. How much work does his push do on the crate?
questions.a: 120 J: work = force x displacement in the direction of the force = 40 N x 3 m.

questions.q: In which of these does the person do positive work on the object?
o: A girl pulls a toy cart forward with a string, and the cart moves forward
A boy holds a heavy bag still at shoulder height
A fielder's hands move back as they stop a moving ball
A waiter carries a tray along a level floor, holding it at the same height
questions.a: Pulling the toy cart forward: the force and the displacement are in the same direction, so the work is positive. Holding still and carrying level give zero work; stopping the ball gives negative work.

questions.q: True or False: 'Work done by a force has no direction; it is described by a number with a positive or a negative sign.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Force and displacement have both magnitude and direction, but work does not have a direction. It is a number that is positive when force and displacement are in the same direction and negative when they are opposite.
s: Reason: work has no direction; its sign shows whether force and displacement are in the same or opposite directions

questions.q: Work done by a force on an object can be zero in three different ways. State each way and give one example of each.
questions.a: (1) The force is zero (F = 0), e.g. a toy car rolling on along a smooth level floor after the push has stopped: no horizontal force acts on it, so no work is done on it along its motion. (2) There is no displacement (s = 0), e.g. pushing a rigid wall that does not move. (3) The force is perpendicular to the displacement, e.g. the upward force of a girl carrying a box while she walks along a level path.
s: Force is zero, with a real example such as a toy car rolling on a smooth level floor with no horizontal force on it
No displacement, with an example such as pushing a rigid wall
Force perpendicular to displacement, with an example such as carrying a box while walking on level ground

questions.q: A boy drags a doormat 2.5 m along the floor at a steady speed with a horizontal force of 16 N. Friction on the mat is also 16 N. (a) Find the work done by the boy on the mat. (b) Find the work done by friction on the mat.
questions.a: (a) The boy's force is along the displacement: W = 16 N x 2.5 m = +40 J. (b) Friction acts opposite to the displacement: W = 16 N x (-2.5 m) = -40 J.
s: (b) work by friction = -40 J, negative because friction is opposite to the displacement

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When a cyclist applies the brakes and her cycle slows down to a stop, the braking force does negative work on the cycle.
Reason (R): The braking force acts opposite to the direction in which the cycle moves.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: work done by a force is negative when the force is opposite to the displacement, which is exactly what R describes.

questions.q: A constant force acting on a block does -48 J of work while the block is displaced 4 m in a straight line. Which describes the force?
o: 12 N, acting opposite to the displacement
192 N, acting opposite to the displacement
44 N, acting opposite to the displacement
questions.a: 12 N acting opposite to the displacement: the negative sign means the force opposes the displacement, and its size is 48 J / 4 m = 12 N.

questions.q: A waiter handles a 2 kg tray (take g = 10 m/s squared, and his upward force equal to the tray's weight). (i) He carries it 8 m along a level floor at the same height. (ii) He lifts it slowly 1.5 m onto a high shelf. (iii) He then holds it still at the shelf for 30 s while a guest takes it. Find the work done by the waiter on the tray in each task, and give the reason for each task in which the work is zero.
questions.a: Weight = 2 kg x 10 m/s squared = 20 N. (i) 0 J. (ii) Force and displacement are both upward: 20 N x 1.5 m = +30 J. (iii) 0 J. Reasons: in (i) the upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement; in (iii) there is no displacement, so no work is done however long he holds it.
s: (ii) +30 J using weight 20 N over 1.5 m
Reasons: (i) force perpendicular to displacement; (iii) no displacement

questions.q: In a warehouse a worker handles a 20 kg box (g = 10 m/s squared; when lifting slowly his force equals its weight). (i) He lifts the box slowly 1.5 m onto a cart. (ii) He pushes the cart with the box 10 m along a smooth floor at steady speed with a force of 40 N, while friction of 40 N acts on the cart. (iii) He then pushes it 5 m across a rough rubber mat at steady speed with a force of 60 N, while friction of 60 N acts on the cart. Find: (a) his work in (i); (b) his work and the work by friction in (ii); (c) his work and the work by friction in (iii); (d) his total work over the whole job; (e) the total work done by friction and the total work done by gravity on the box over the whole job.
questions.a: (a) 200 N x 1.5 m = +300 J. (b) Worker: 40 N x 10 m = +400 J; friction: 40 N x (-10 m) = -400 J. (c) Worker: 60 N x 5 m = +300 J; friction: 60 N x (-5 m) = -300 J. (d) 300 + 400 + 300 = +1000 J. (e) Friction: -400 J + (-300 J) = -700 J. Gravity does -300 J while the box rises and 0 J on both level pushes (perpendicular to the displacement), so -300 J in all.
s: (b) +400 J by the worker and -400 J by friction
(c) +300 J by the worker and -300 J by friction
(d) total work by the worker = +1000 J
(e) friction -700 J in all; gravity -300 J (only the lift counts)

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about work.
I. The SI unit of work is the joule.
II. No work is done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement of the object.
III. 1 J of work is done when a constant force of 1 N displaces an object by 1 m in the direction of the force.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III. The joule is the SI unit of work, a force perpendicular to the displacement does no work, and 1 J = 1 N x 1 m when the displacement is in the direction of the force.

questions.q: An object that has the capacity to do work is said to possess
questions.a: Energy: an object having the capacity to do work is said to possess energy.

questions.q: Which pair of quantities has the same SI unit?
questions.a: Work and energy: both are measured in joules (J). Power is in watts and force in newtons.

questions.q:
Match each device or process (Column I) with the energy change in it (Column II).
Column I: 1. A glowing bulb  2. An electric water heater  3. Food powering our muscles  4. A ringing bell
Column II: A. Mechanical to sound  B. Electrical to light  C. Chemical to mechanical  D. Electrical to thermal
questions.a: 1-B, 2-D, 3-C, 4-A: a bulb changes electrical energy into light, a water heater changes electrical energy into thermal energy of the water, the chemical energy of food is changed into mechanical energy by our muscles, and a ringing bell changes mechanical energy into sound.

questions.q: What is meant by energy? State the work-energy theorem.
questions.a: Energy is the capacity to do work. Work-energy theorem: the work done on an object equals the change in its energy.
s: Energy is the capacity to do work
Work done on an object = change in its energy

questions.q: Name the form of energy described in each case. (a) Energy stored in fuels and food in the chemical bonds between atoms. (b) Energy of the vibrations of air or other molecules. (c) Energy stored in the nuclei of atoms.
questions.a: (a) Chemical energy. (b) Sound energy. (c) Nuclear energy.

questions.q: True or False: 'When a moving trolley runs into a heavy sandbag and comes to a stop, the trolley's energy decreases.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The sandbag pushes on the trolley opposite to its displacement, so it does negative work on the trolley, and by the work-energy theorem negative work done on the trolley decreases its energy.
s: Reason: the sandbag does negative work on the trolley, and work done equals the change in energy, so its energy falls

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The work-energy theorem can be used even when the force on an object is not constant.
Reason (R): The work-energy theorem holds only for a single object and never for a system of objects.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the theorem holds when the forces are not constant and also for a system of objects.

questions.q: A cart has 10 J of energy. A boy's push then does +40 J of work on it while friction does -16 J of work on it. (a) Find the cart's energy afterwards. (b) Find the total work done on the cart.
questions.a: (a) Energy afterwards = 10 J + 40 J - 16 J = 34 J. (b) Total work = +40 J - 16 J = +24 J, which equals the change in energy, 34 J - 10 J.
s: (b) total work = +24 J, equal to the change in energy

questions.q: Sameer says, 'The water standing still behind a high dam has no energy, because it is not moving.' Is he right? Explain using the idea of energy as the capacity to do work.
questions.a: No. If the water is let out, it falls and can push on the blades of a turbine and make them move, so it has the capacity to do work, which means it has energy. This energy is due to its raised position (its height above the turbine), not its motion: it is potential energy.
s: The water can do work (push and move a turbine) when it falls, so it has energy
The energy is due to its raised position (potential energy), not motion

questions.q: At a school science fair, Divya builds a chain of energy changes. A battery runs a small electric motor. The motor winds a string that lifts a 0.5 kg weight slowly through 0.4 m, so the force on the weight equals its weight. The weight is then released, falls back and strikes a bell. The bell rings only if the weight strikes it with at least 1.5 J of kinetic energy. Take g = 10 m/s squared and ignore air resistance. (a) Name the energy change in the motor. (b) Find the work done by the string on the weight in the 0.4 m lift. (c) In what form is this energy stored at the top, and how much kinetic energy does the weight have just before it strikes the bell? (d) To save the battery, Divya wants to lift the weight only 0.25 m or 0.35 m. Find the least height that still rings the bell and decide which of the two heights she should use.
questions.a: (a) Electrical energy to mechanical energy. (b) W = 0.5 kg x 10 m/s squared x 0.4 m = 2 J. (c) It is stored as potential energy because of the raised position; as it falls this becomes kinetic energy, so it has 2 J just before striking. (d) Least height h = 1.5 J / (0.5 kg x 10 m/s squared) = 0.3 m. At 0.25 m the weight gets only 1.25 J, which is less than 1.5 J, so the bell does not ring; at 0.35 m it gets 1.75 J, so the bell rings. She should use 0.35 m.
s: (c) stored as potential energy; 2 J of kinetic energy before striking
(d) least height 0.3 m (1.25 J vs 1.75 J); choose 0.35 m

questions.q: The energy possessed by an object because of its motion is called
questions.a: Kinetic energy: the energy an object has due to its motion.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball rolls along the ground at 3 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.a: 9 J: K = 1/2 x m x v squared = 1/2 x 2 kg x (3 m/s) squared = 9 J.

questions.q: True or False: 'The kinetic energy of a moving bus has a direction, the same as the direction of the bus's velocity.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. Kinetic energy has no direction. It depends only on the mass and the magnitude of the velocity, K = 1/2 m v squared, and is measured in joules.
s: Reason: kinetic energy has no direction; K = 1/2 m v squared depends only on mass and speed

questions.q: What happens to the kinetic energy of a moving object in each case? (a) Positive work is done on it and its velocity increases. (b) Negative work is done on it and its velocity decreases. (c) No work is done on it and its velocity does not change.
questions.a: (a) Its kinetic energy increases. (b) Its kinetic energy decreases. (c) Its kinetic energy stays constant.

questions.q: A 0.5 kg ball rolls across a playground at 4 m/s. (i) Write the formula for kinetic energy. (ii) Find the ball's kinetic energy. (iii) Find its kinetic energy if its speed becomes 8 m/s. (iv) How many times did the kinetic energy increase when the speed doubled? (v) Find the kinetic energy of a 1 kg ball rolling at 4 m/s.
questions.a: (i) K = 1/2 m v squared. (ii) K = 1/2 x 0.5 x 4 x 4 = 4 J. (iii) K = 1/2 x 0.5 x 8 x 8 = 16 J. (iv) 16 J / 4 J = 4 times. (v) K = 1/2 x 1 x 4 x 4 = 8 J.

questions.q: A 50 kg girl running on a track has 400 J of kinetic energy. (a) Find her speed. (b) Find her kinetic energy if she slows to half that speed.
questions.a: (a) 400 = 1/2 x 50 x v squared, so v squared = 16 and v = 4 m/s. (b) At 2 m/s, K = 1/2 x 50 x 2 x 2 = 100 J (one quarter of 400 J).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about kinetic energy.
I. If the mass of an object is doubled at the same speed, its kinetic energy doubles.
II. If the speed of an object is halved, its kinetic energy becomes half.
III. An object at rest has zero kinetic energy.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed, so halving the speed makes it one quarter.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A 0.2 kg ball moving at 30 m/s has more kinetic energy than a 0.4 kg ball moving at 15 m/s.
Reason (R): Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed, so doubling the speed has a bigger effect than doubling the mass.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The first ball has 1/2 x 0.2 x 900 = 90 J and the second 1/2 x 0.4 x 225 = 45 J: doubling the mass only doubles the kinetic energy, but doubling the speed makes it four times as large.

questions.q: A 1200 kg car has 60000 J of kinetic energy. (a) Find its speed in m/s. (b) Express this speed in km/h. (c) Find its kinetic energy if its speed doubles.
questions.a: (a) 60000 = 1/2 x 1200 x v squared, so v squared = 100 and v = 10 m/s. (b) 10 m/s x 3.6 = 36 km/h. (c) Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy 4 times: 240000 J.

questions.q: A 40 kg trolley is already moving at 3 m/s on a smooth level floor. A worker pushes it forward with a constant force of 60 N over 10 m (ignore friction). (i) Find its kinetic energy before the push. (ii) Find the work done by the push. (iii) Find its kinetic energy after the push. (iv) Find its speed after the push. (v) If the same push acted on the trolley starting from rest, its final speed would be about 5.5 m/s. Compare the gain in speed in the two cases and explain why the same work gives a smaller gain when the trolley is already moving.
questions.a: (i) K = 1/2 x 40 x 3 x 3 = 180 J. (ii) W = 60 N x 10 m = 600 J. (iii) By the work-energy theorem, K = 180 J + 600 J = 780 J. (iv) 780 = 1/2 x 40 x v squared, so v squared = 39 and v is about 6.2 m/s. (v) Moving trolley gains about 6.2 - 3 = 3.2 m/s; from rest it gains about 5.5 m/s. The work adds the same 600 J of energy each time, but kinetic energy depends on v squared, so at a higher speed the same added energy raises the speed by less.
s: (v) gains of about 3.2 m/s and 5.5 m/s compared, explained by K depending on v squared

questions.q: A slingshot (gulel) band is stretched and held still. What kind of energy does the stretched band have?
o: Potential energy due to its changed shape
Kinetic energy due to its motion
Sound energy due to its vibration
Nuclear energy stored in its atoms
questions.a: Potential energy due to its changed shape: a deformed object stores the work done in deforming it.

questions.q: A 3 kg box of tiles is kept on a terrace 4 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s squared and the ground as the zero level, what is its potential energy?
questions.a: 120 J: U = mgh = 3 kg x 10 m/s squared x 4 m.

questions.q: Define potential energy. Give one example of energy stored by deformation and one example of energy stored because of the relative positions of objects.
questions.a: Potential energy is the energy stored by an object as a result of its deformation, or in a system of objects due to their relative positions. Deformation: a compressed spring or a bent bow. Relative position: two separated unlike magnetic poles, or a ball lifted above the Earth.
s: Definition: energy stored due to deformation or relative positions of objects in a system
One correct example of each kind

questions.q: True or False: 'When the same ball is raised to a greater height above the ground, its potential energy increases.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Raising the ball higher needs more work against gravity, and that work is stored as potential energy (U = mgh grows with h). In Activity 7.1 a ball dropped from a greater height makes a deeper depression in sand.
s: Reason: more work is done to raise it higher, so U = mgh is larger (deeper sand depression)

questions.q: A pendulum bob is pulled to one side to point P and released. It swings through its lowest point Q and stops for a moment at point R on the other side. Ignoring friction, state the kind of energy the bob has at (a) P, (b) Q and (c) R.
questions.a: (a) At P: only potential energy, no kinetic energy. (b) At Q: only kinetic energy, no potential energy (taking Q as the zero level). (c) At R: only potential energy again, no kinetic energy.

questions.q: Take g = 10 m/s squared. (a) A 2 kg bag on a shelf has 60 J of potential energy. How high is the shelf? (b) What mass placed 1.5 m above the ground would have the same 60 J of potential energy?
A 2 kg stone is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s squared, what are its kinetic and potential energies when it has fallen 5 m?
questions.a: Kinetic 100 J, potential 300 J: mechanical energy stays 2 x 10 x 20 = 400 J; at 15 m the potential energy is 2 x 10 x 15 = 300 J, so the kinetic energy is 400 - 300 = 100 J.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Just before a freely falling ball dropped from height h hits the ground, its kinetic energy is zero (ignoring air resistance).
Reason (R): The mechanical energy of a freely falling ball stays equal to mgh throughout its fall (ignoring air resistance).
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: mechanical energy is conserved, so it stays mgh, but just before landing the potential energy is zero and all of mgh is kinetic energy, so the kinetic energy is at its largest, not zero.

questions.q: A water park in Pune has two slides. The tall slide starts 5 m above the pool and the short slide 3.2 m above it. A 30 kg child starts from rest at the top. Treat the slides as frictionless and take g = 10 m/s squared. (a) Find the child's potential energy at the top of the tall slide. (b) Find the child's speed at the bottom of the tall slide. (c) The park wants a small slide for toddlers that gives a speed of 4 m/s at the bottom. How high should it start? (d) The park's safety rule allows children under 10 only on slides that give a speed of no more than 9 m/s at the bottom. Find the speed at the bottom of the short slide and decide which of the two slides children under 10 may use.
questions.a: (a) U = 30 x 10 x 5 = 1500 J. (b) All of it becomes kinetic energy: 1/2 x 30 x v squared = 1500, so v squared = 100 and v = 10 m/s. (c) From mgh = 1/2 m v squared, h = v squared / 2g = 16 / 20 = 0.8 m. (d) v = square root of (2 x 10 x 3.2) = square root of 64 = 8 m/s. 8 m/s is within 9 m/s but the tall slide's 10 m/s is not, so children under 10 may use only the short slide.
s: (b) 10 m/s from mgh = 1/2 m v squared
(d) 8 m/s on the short slide; only the short slide meets the 9 m/s rule

questions.q: A 0.4 kg ball is thrown straight up at 15 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s squared. (i) Find its kinetic energy at launch. (ii) Ignoring air resistance, find the greatest height it reaches. (iii) Ignoring air resistance, find its speed when it is 5 m above the launch point. (iv) In fact the ball reaches only 10 m. Find its potential energy at that height. (v) Find the work done by air resistance on the way up.
questions.a: (i) K = 1/2 x 0.4 x 15 x 15 = 45 J. (ii) At the top all 45 J is potential energy: h = 45 / (0.4 x 10) = 11.25 m. (iii) At 5 m, U = 0.4 x 10 x 5 = 20 J, so K = 45 - 20 = 25 J and v = square root of (2 x 25 / 0.4) = square root of 125, about 11.2 m/s. (iv) U = 0.4 x 10 x 10 = 40 J. (v) Mechanical energy fell from 45 J to 40 J, so by the work-energy theorem air resistance did -5 J of work.
s: (v) -5 J of work by air resistance

questions.q: What is the SI unit of power?
questions.a: The watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J of work done per second.

questions.q: An electric motor does 3000 J of work in 15 s. What is its power?
Define power and write its formula. Name the SI unit of power.
questions.a: Power is the rate at which work is done: P = W / t. Its SI unit is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.
s: Power is the rate of doing work, P = W / t
SI unit: the watt, 1 W = 1 J/s

questions.q: A machine does 2400 J of work in 2 minutes. (a) Write the time in seconds. (b) Find the power of the machine.
True or False: '1 watt is the power when 1 joule of work is done in 1 second.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Power = work / time, so 1 J of work in 1 s gives 1 J/s, which is defined as 1 watt.
s: Reason: P = W / t, so 1 J / 1 s = 1 J/s = 1 W

questions.q: At a construction site, a small hoist lifts a 30 kg box of tiles steadily through 2 m in 4 s. Take g = 10 m/s squared. (a) Find the weight of the box. (b) Find the work done in lifting it. (c) Find the power of the hoist. (d) Find the power needed to do the same lift in 2 s.

Consider the following statements about power.
I. 1 W is the same as 1 J s^-1.
II. A machine that does 1200 J of work in 4 s has more power than one that does 2000 J in 8 s.
III. If the same work is done in half the time, the power is halved.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. In II the powers are 300 W and 250 W. Statement III is wrong: doing the same work in half the time doubles the power.

questions.q: Four water pumps are tested. Pump A does 4000 J of work in 8 s, B does 2700 J in 6 s, C does 1500 J in 2.5 s and D does 1000 J in 2 s. Which pump is the most powerful?
questions.a: Pump C: its power is 1500 / 2.5 = 600 W, against 500 W for A, 450 W for B and 500 W for D.

questions.q: A lift cabin of mass 500 kg carries 4 people of 60 kg each up through 12 m at steady speed in 15 s. Take g = 10 m/s squared and ignore friction. (a) Find the total mass lifted. (b) Find the work done by the motor. (c) Find the power of the motor.

On sports day in a Bhopal school, two students race up the stadium staircase, which rises 12 m. Kiran has a mass of 50 kg and reaches the top in 20 s. Arif has a mass of 60 kg and takes 30 s. Take g = 10 m/s squared and count only the work done against gravity. (a) Find the work done by Kiran. (b) Find Kiran's power. (c) Find the work done and the power of Arif. (d) Decide who did more work and who was more powerful, and explain why the answers differ.
questions.a: (a) W = 50 x 10 x 12 = 6000 J. (b) P = 6000 J / 20 s = 300 W. (c) Arif: W = 60 x 10 x 12 = 7200 J; P = 7200 J / 30 s = 240 W. (d) Arif did more work (7200 J against 6000 J) because he is heavier, but Kiran was more powerful (300 W against 240 W) because she did her work in less time; power depends on both the work and the time.
s: (c) Arif's work 7200 J and power 240 W
(d) Arif did more work, Kiran was more powerful, with the reason (power = work / time)

questions.q: The mechanical advantage of a simple machine is defined as
questions.a: Load divided by effort: mechanical advantage = load / effort.

questions.q:
Match each part of a lever (Column I) with its meaning (Column II).
Column I: 1. Fulcrum  2. Load  3. Effort  4. Effort arm
Column II: A. The force applied  B. The distance of the effort from the fulcrum  C. The fixed point about which the lever rotates  D. The force to be overcome
questions.a: 1-C, 2-D, 3-A, 4-B: the fulcrum is the fixed turning point, the load is the force to be overcome, the effort is the force applied and the effort arm is the distance of the effort from the fulcrum.

questions.q: In a pair of tweezers, the fingers press at a point between the joined end (the fulcrum) and the tips that grip the object (the load). To which class of lever do tweezers belong?
questions.a: Class III: the effort is in between the fulcrum and the load.

questions.q: True or False: 'A simple machine reduces the total work needed to lift a load.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. A simple machine only changes the magnitude or the direction of the force needed. The total work stays the same: a smaller effort has to move through a larger distance. Machines do not create energy.
s: Reason: it changes only the size or direction of the force; a smaller force acts over a larger distance, so the work is the same

questions.q: A smooth ramp 3 m long is used to push a 400 N box onto a platform 0.6 m high (ignore friction). (a) Find the mechanical advantage of the ramp. (b) Find the effort needed. (c) Find the effort needed if a 6 m long ramp is used to reach the same platform.
questions.a: (a) MA = L / h = 3 m / 0.6 m = 5. (b) Effort = load / MA = 400 N / 5 = 80 N. (c) MA = 6 / 0.6 = 10, so effort = 400 N / 10 = 40 N.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A worker raises a 600 N load by pulling with an effort of only 300 N on a pulley arrangement, so the arrangement cannot be a single fixed pulley.
Reason (R): A single fixed pulley only changes the direction of the effort, so its mechanical advantage is 1.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the arrangement has MA = 600 N / 300 N = 2, but a single fixed pulley has MA 1 (effort equals load), so it must include a movable pulley.

questions.q: A labourer uses a crowbar to move a 600 N rock. The load arm is 0.2 m and the effort arm is 1.2 m. What effort is needed?
questions.a: 100 N: effort x effort arm = load x load arm, so effort = 600 N x 0.2 m / 1.2 m.

questions.q: A school must help a wheelchair user over a step 0.5 m high. The wheelchair with its rider weighs 800 N. It can build a smooth ramp either 4 m long or 5 m long. Ignore friction. (a) Find the push needed along the 4 m ramp. (b) Find the push needed along the 5 m ramp. (c) Which ramp should the school build so that the push is smaller? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) MA = L / h = 4 / 0.5 = 8, so the push = 800 N / 8 = 100 N. (b) MA = 5 / 0.5 = 10, so the push = 800 N / 10 = 80 N. (c) The 5 m ramp: it is longer and less steep for the same height, so its mechanical advantage is larger and a smaller push is needed.
s: (c) the 5 m ramp, because the longer, less steep ramp has the larger mechanical advantage

questions.q: A gardener must lift a 900 N stone, but she can push down with at most 150 N. She uses a 2.1 m iron bar resting on a small rock as the fulcrum, with the stone at one end and her hands at the other. (a) Find the mechanical advantage she needs. (b) Where should the fulcrum be placed along the bar? (c) Name the class of this lever. (d) If she moves the rock a little closer to the stone, will the effort she needs increase or decrease? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) MA = 900 N / 150 N = 6. (b) Effort arm / load arm = 6 and the two add to 2.1 m, so load arm = 0.3 m and effort arm = 1.8 m: the fulcrum is 0.3 m from the stone. (c) Class I, since the fulcrum is between the load and the effort. (d) It decreases: the load arm gets shorter and the effort arm longer, so the mechanical advantage (effort arm / load arm) becomes larger than 6 and less than 150 N is needed.
s: (b) fulcrum 0.3 m from the stone (load arm 0.3 m, effort arm 1.8 m)
(d) effort decreases, because the load arm shortens and the effort arm lengthens, raising the MA

questions.q: A shopkeeper needs to raise a 500 N sack onto a cart 1.2 m high. She can apply an effort of at most 200 N. She has three choices: (A) a single fixed pulley, (B) a smooth ramp 3.6 m long, and (C) a pulley system with a mechanical advantage of 2. Ignore friction. (i) Find the effort needed with the fixed pulley. (ii) Find the mechanical advantage and the effort needed with the ramp. (iii) Find the effort needed with the pulley system. (iv) Decide which choice or choices she can use. (v) Find the work she does with the choice you picked, and compare it with the work needed to lift the sack straight up.
questions.a: (i) A fixed pulley has MA = 1, so the effort is 500 N. (ii) Ramp MA = L / h = 3.6 / 1.2 = 3, so effort = 500 / 3, about 167 N. (iii) Effort = 500 N / 2 = 250 N. (iv) Only the ramp needs less than 200 N, so she should use the ramp. (v) Work along the ramp = (500/3) N x 3.6 m = 600 J, which equals 500 N x 1.2 m = 600 J for a straight lift: the ramp reduces the force, not the work.
s: (iv) chooses the ramp as the only choice under 200 N
(v) 600 J, the same as lifting straight up
